source.title: Reliability of CKA as a Similarity Measure in Deep Learning
source.authors: Mohammad-Javad Davari; Stefan Horoi; A. Natik; Guillaume Lajoie; Guy Wolf; Eugene Belilovsky

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own analyses showing that CKA can change sharply under representation transformations and can be manipulated while task performance changes little. This challenges unqualified conclusions drawn from CKA similarity, and refines the claim to depend on the metric and its settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's main results concern CKA sensitivity and manipulation, not whether alignment between independently trained models rises with scale or performance. It does not test the cross-modal, feature-universality, or general interchangeability versions. Values read only from plots are marked figure only; layerwise maps and supplementary figures are not exhaustively transcribed.
record.test_reason: A metric critique of CKA, not a measurement of convergence. Only the cross-network early-layer comparisons (generalized vs memorized vs random CNNs) bear on V6. There, CKA reports high similarity while filters and linear-probe accuracy show different, unequally useful features, so the similarity conclusion depends on the measure. The other experiments compare a representation with an altered copy of itself, or optimize within-network CKA maps on purpose. They show CKA sensitivity in general, not cross-model convergence, and fit no version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also show that RBF CKA can be manipulated, and that functional behaviour holds on CIFAR-10-C. They state they do not intend to cast doubt on CKA generally. They urge caution, especially with pre-trained models of unknown provenance, and recommend using multiple measures.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear CKA and RBF CKA, but studies representation transformations, metric sensitivity, and CKA-map optimization rather than testing scale-dependent convergence between models.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with the representation transformation and with RBF bandwidth; σ = 0.2 × median distance is reported as unperturbed by the synthetic subset translation, while larger bandwidth settings are sensitive.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear and RBF CKA between a representation and a translated or linearly transformed copy of itself falls toward 0, while separability and local geometry are preserved. RBF with σ=0.2×median is unaffected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CKA similarity is highly sensitive to subset translations, outliers and invertible linear transforms, and the sensitivity depends on kernel bandwidth.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-network CKA maps can be optimized to arbitrary targets, including removing width-associated block structure, with accuracy changes under about 1 point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CKA maps can be manipulated with little change to model function, so CKA structure need not reflect functional differences.

record.problems: Many CKA outcomes are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. Several experiments use deliberately modified representations or CKA-map optimization, so they establish metric sensitivity under those interventions rather than natural convergence patterns across models. The paper does not test scale or cross-modal convergence.
record.rows_left_out: Not exhaustively transcribed: separate per-layer CKA values in Figures 2 and 15; additional target-map and kernel-bandwidth configurations in Figures 6, 12, 13, and 14; supplementary width and shifted-data maps in Figures 10–11; and OOD accuracy results in Figure 17. These are omitted because their CKA values are figure-only or add further instances of the already recorded metric-manipulation findings.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep across independently trained, different-architecture models.
No vision–language or paired image–caption comparison.
Fig. 15 shows same- and different-seed CKA only for early layers and only as plots. Shared features or subspaces across seeds are not tested.
No stitching, linear mapping or relative-representation tests between models.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features or circuits.

No comparison of convergence trends across many similarity measures, no neighbourhood-size settings, and no out-of-distribution effects on cross-model alignment. Fig. 10 OOD maps concern manipulated within-network maps only.
No test of plateaus, completeness, or shared data or objectives as the cause of alignment.

missing.what: Generalized vs generalized network CKA in early layers, with the same and with different random seeds (figure-only values)
Linear-probe accuracy on early layers for generalized, memorized and random networks; the evidence the R7/R8 verdict rests on

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every row to V6. Most rows are self-vs-transformed-copy comparisons or deliberate CKA-map optimizations, so they were unlinked and moved to fits_no_version. The reader's limits_scope label for R3 was backwards: the bandwidth dependence it shows is evidence of setting dependence. The only V6 verdict rests on figure-only rows. Not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep testing whether independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data become more aligned.
No paired image-caption comparison or vision-language model performance sweep.
The paper compares some networks with same and different random seeds, but does not test whether same-architecture networks converge on shared features or subspaces across seeds.
The transformations studied are not tests of mapping one model's representations onto another's by stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
No recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits are tested.

Tests sensitivity of CKA to transformations of representations and to RBF bandwidth choices. It does not systematically compare a broad range of similarity measures or out-of-distribution inputs for convergence between independently trained models.
The study does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment, nor measure whether cross-model alignment plateaus or remains incomplete.

rows.subject: Artificial representations X and subset-translated Y
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear CKA as one of two linearly separable point groups was translated.

conditions.value: 10K points from each of two unit cubes; centers separated along the first dimension
second cube translated in a random direction; distance varied
linear

rows.measure: Linear CKA between original and translated representations
rows.value: CKA quickly fell below 0.2 as translation distance increased.
rows.note: The authors state that this transformation preserves within-group local geometry and the separation of the two groups.
rows.check: Synthetic points compared with a translated copy of themselves. No independently trained models, so not a convergence measurement. This is a general CKA-sensitivity result.

rows.subject: Artificial representations X and subset-translated Y
rows.operation_detail: Measured RBF CKA as one of two linearly separable point groups was translated.

conditions.value: 10K points from each of two unit cubes; centers separated along the first dimension
second cube translated in a random direction; distance varied
RBF; bandwidth settings shown in Figure 4a other than 0.2 times median distance

rows.measure: RBF CKA between original and translated representations
rows.value: For the plotted RBF settings other than 0.2 times median distance, CKA quickly fell below 0.2 as translation increased.
rows.note: The paper explicitly says the 0.2-times-median setting is unperturbed; that setting is recorded separately in R3.
rows.check: Same synthetic self-vs-transformed-copy setup as R1. Not a cross-model convergence measurement.

rows.subject: Artificial representations X and subset-translated Y

conditions.value: 10K points from each of two unit cubes
second cube translated in a random direction; distance varied
RBF; σ = 0.2 × median distance between examples

rows.measure: RBF CKA between original and translated representations
rows.value: The CKA value was unperturbed by the transformation.
rows.note: The authors characterize this small-bandwidth setting as less informative than larger bandwidth settings.
rows.check: Synthetic self-comparison. The original state 'absent' and the limits_scope label had the direction wrong. Together with R2, the bandwidth dependence this row shows is evidence of setting dependence, not a limit on it.

conditions.value: CIFAR10 training-set representations at the last layer before output
whole-class translation preserving linear separability; distance varied

rows.measure: Linear CKA between original and modified representations
rows.value: CKA quickly dropped to 0 as translation distance increased.
rows.note: The authors report that a linear classifier classified both sets with greater than 90% accuracy.
rows.check: One CNN's representations compared with a manually translated copy. Not two independently trained models.

rows.subject: 9-layer CNN trained on CIFAR10
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear CKA after translating a single representation.

conditions.value: CIFAR10 training-set representations at the last layer before output
one point translated; translation distance varied

rows.measure: Linear CKA between original and modified representations
rows.value: CKA dropped substantially as the single point was moved; the plotted value approaches 0.
rows.note: The text emphasizes that a single point among tens of thousands can strongly influence CKA.
rows.check: Single-point outlier translation of one model's representations. A self-comparison, not convergence.

rows.subject: Artificial representations X and Y = XM
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear CKA after multiplying X by a sampled invertible matrix M.

conditions.value: M entries sampled from a Gaussian with mean μ and standard deviation σ; only invertible matrices retained
small μ and σ

rows.measure: Linear CKA between X and Y = XM
rows.value: CKA dropped to 0 even for small μ and σ.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation across 10 random instantiations are shown; numerical uncertainty values not stated.
rows.note: The figure varies μ and σ; the text describes the result as occurring even for small values.
rows.check: Synthetic X vs XM invertible transform. Not a model comparison.

rows.subject: Generalized and memorized CIFAR10 networks
rows.stage_stated: generalized network trained on CIFAR10; memorized network trained with random target labels
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise CKA for early layers.

conditions.value: generalized vs. memorized
early layers

rows.value: Early layers had relatively high CKA, although the paper describes their filters as drastically different and their features as not equally useful.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation across 5 seeds shown; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The paper also reports that linear-probe accuracy differs across these networks, but does not give numerical values in the text.
rows.check: Values are figure-only (Fig. 2, 15). Linear CKA is relatively high while filters (Fig. 3) and probe accuracy (Fig. 16) differ. The state should be observed for V6, not partial: the conclusion depends on which measure is used.

rows.subject: ResNet-34 CIFAR10 networks of different widths
rows.size_stated: ResNet-34; width x2, x4, and x5
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR10, then CKA-map optimized
rows.operation_detail: Optimized wider networks' CKA maps to resemble the width-x1 target map.

conditions.value: width-x1 network CKA map
x2, x4, and x5

rows.measure: CKA map similarity to target; test performance
rows.baseline: Original maps shown in Figure 7; target width-x1 accuracy 93.7%.
rows.value: Optimized maps nearly matched the thinner target map (map values figure only); accuracies x2 93.3%, x4 94.1%, x5 93.2%.
rows.note: The authors state that width-associated CKA structures could be removed without substantially changing performance.
rows.check: Wider networks optimized to mimic a thin network's CKA map. This is an induced manipulation of within-network maps, not natural cross-model alignment.

relationships.condition: Early layers of 9-layer CIFAR10 CNNs: generalized vs memorized, and generalized vs untrained random
relationships.reason: Linear CKA is relatively high, yet filters and linear-probe accuracy show different, unequally useful features. Cross-network similarity conclusions therefore depend on the measure (R7, R8; figure-only).
relationships.display_finding: Linear CKA remained relatively high despite filter differences and unequal linear-probe accuracy between generalizing, memorizing and random networks.
